summary.text: The Aufbau principle says that in an atom's or ion's ground state, electrons first fill the lowest-energy subshells and then move on to higher-energy ones.
Filling this way gives the most stable electron configuration possible, so the 1s subshell fills before the 2s.
Subshells fill in order of increasing n + ℓ, and when that sum ties, the subshell with the lower n goes first.

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: German for 'building-up principle', not a scientist's name

facts.label: Rule-breaking elements
facts.value: Twenty elements differ from the Madelung prediction

items.prompt: An atom is building up past argon. Subshell A has n = 4 and ℓ = 0, while subshell B has n = 3 and ℓ = 2. Which fills first, and why?

options.label: A, because its n + ℓ sum is lower
B, because its n value is lower
Neither, since both fill at the same moment
B, because it can hold more electrons

items.explain: A has n + ℓ = 4 and B has n + ℓ = 5, and subshells with a lower n + ℓ value are filled first.

items.prompt: Two subshells end up with exactly the same n + ℓ value. How is the tie settled?

options.label: The one with the higher n fills first
They share electrons equally between them
The one with the lower n fills first
The one with the higher ℓ fills first

items.explain: Where n + ℓ values are equal, the subshell with the lower n value is filled first.

items.prompt: Three orbitals of equal energy are open and three electrons arrive in them. How do the electrons settle?

options.label: Two share one orbital and the third takes another
Each takes its own orbital, all with the same spin
Each takes its own orbital, with spins alternating
All three crowd into the lowest of the orbitals

items.explain: Hund's rule says electrons occupy different orbitals of the same energy singly, with the same spin, before any are occupied doubly.

items.prompt: Copper's measured configuration differs from what the n + ℓ ordering predicts for it. Why does the real atom take that other arrangement?

options.label: The ordering rule only applies to atoms in an excited state
A copper atom always has one fewer electron than expected
Experiments in the lab disturb the electrons while measuring
Filling its d subshell puts the atom in a lower energy state

items.explain: By filling the 3d subshell, copper can be in a lower energy state, so the measured form is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ rather than the predicted [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s².

The exceptions only appear in atoms that carry a positive charge

paragraphs.heading: What it says
paragraphs.text: The Aufbau principle, from the German for 'building-up principle', says that when an atom or ion is in its ground state, its electrons fill the lowest-energy subshells first and only then move to higher ones. So the 1s subshell fills before any electron goes into 2s. Filling this way gives the atom or ion the most stable electron configuration it can have.

paragraphs.heading: Where it came from
paragraphs.text: The name describes the idea rather than honouring a scientist. Niels Bohr formulated the principle in the early 1920s. It was an early use of quantum mechanics on electrons, and it explained chemical properties in physical terms. Each new electron added to an atom feels the electric field set up by the positive nucleus and by the negative electrons already bound to it.

paragraphs.heading: The n + ℓ rule
paragraphs.text: In practice, electrons go into subshells in order of increasing n + ℓ. Here n is the principal quantum number and ℓ is the azimuthal quantum number, with ℓ = 0, 1, 2, 3 standing for s, p, d and f. When two subshells share the same n + ℓ, the one with lower n fills first. That gives a sequence that begins 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p and carries on from there.

paragraphs.heading: Zinc as an example
paragraphs.text: Zinc shows the rule at work: its full configuration reads 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d¹⁰. To save space, the core electrons are often swapped for the symbol of the previous noble gas in square brackets, leaving only the valence electrons written out. For zinc that gas is argon, so the configuration shortens to [Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰.

paragraphs.heading: Partner rules
paragraphs.text: Other principles fill in how electrons behave. Hund's rule says that when several orbitals have the same energy, electrons take separate orbitals one at a time, with the same spin, before any orbital gets two. If two electrons do share an orbital, the Pauli exclusion principle demands that their spins differ, +1⁄2 and −1⁄2.

paragraphs.heading: Where it breaks
paragraphs.text: This energy ordering, known as the Madelung rule, holds only for neutral atoms that are in their ground state, and one textbook calls it essentially an approximate rule drawn from observation. For twenty elements its prediction differs from what experiments find. Copper is one example: the rule predicts [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s², but the measured configuration is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. By filling the 3d subshell, copper can sit in a lower energy state.

paragraphs.heading: Why the exceptions matter little
paragraphs.text: These exceptions are not very important for chemistry, because the energy differences are small and a nearby atom can change which configuration is preferred. The periodic table ignores them and follows idealized configurations. They arise from repulsion between electrons, and most of them vanish when atoms become positive ions.
